title: Three lines of teaching
hookLine: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind: the teaching of the Buddhas (Dhammapada 183)
tomorrow: is wanting more a problem, or the point?

lines: EXPLAIN YOUR JOB IN FIVE WORDS.
cards: There's a game at parties: explain your job in five words. It is harder than it sounds. Now try a whole religion in three short lines.
Verse one eighty-three does it, and says so boldly. In plain words: avoid all evil, do good, purify your own mind; this is the teaching of the Buddhas. Not of one Buddha.
Of the Buddhas. That's the odd part. If it's that simple, why does the rest of the book exist?

teach.h: THE MASTER IN THE PINE TREE.
teach.b: A story from Chinese Buddhism answers it. A well-known poet named Bai Juyi was sent to govern a district. He'd heard of a Chan master who meditated high in a pine tree, so people called him Bird's Nest.
The poet stood underneath and called up: isn't that dangerous? The master called down: you're in more danger than I am. Then the poet asked for the heart of the Buddha's teaching.
Bird's Nest answered with the verse's opening lines: do no evil, do only good. The poet laughed.

teach.h: AN OLD MAN CAN'T DO IT.
teach.b: And the master said: a child may know it, but an old man still can't do it. That's the puzzle solved. The lines are short because they're easy to know.
The rest of the book exists because they're hard to do. Then what Buddhists do with it.
In the Theravada tradition these verses are remembered as the Ovada Patimokkha, the Buddha's core admonition, and tradition says he first spoke them to a great gathering of his disciples.
Some Buddhist communities celebrate that day as Magha Puja, chanting these lines and walking with candles around a shrine. And notice the order.
Avoid comes first, then do, then purify. Stop the harm before you add the good, and keep going inward.

how: Theravada Buddhists remember Dhammapada 183–185 as the Ovada Patimokkha; in some countries Magha Puja is kept with chanting and a candlelit walk around a temple or shrine.

games.q: what does “three lines of teaching” mean?
o: the three times of day Buddhists chant
avoid evil, do good, and purify the mind
three vows a monk takes on entering a monastery

games.q: the three lines and the tree: tap the pairs.
p: the Chan master who sat in a pine tree
the poet who said a child knows that
a day of chanting and candles

s: the three lines are short because the teaching is simple to live
easy to know, hard to do: a child may know it, but an old man still can't do it.
the verse calls itself the teaching of the Buddhas, not of one Buddha
the verse itself says the Buddhas, plural: a teaching held in common, not one man's idea.
Buddhism's summary is just: be kind and don't overthink it
it has three parts in order: avoid evil, do good, and purify your own mind.

games.q: you're the master in the tree. the governor laughs: a small child knows avoid evil, do good. what do you say?
o: a child may know it, but an old man still can't do it.
then you must be a child, if that's all you understood.
there's a deeper secret meaning only monks are told.
games.why: knowing isn't doing. the lines are short so anyone can know them; the practice of a lifetime is living them.

practice: Make a small plan for today in three parts. One thing to avoid: a habit, a word, a click. One good thing to do: small and specific.
One way to clear the mind: a minute of quiet, a walk, a slower breath. Hold the three in turn while you sit, then let them rest.

wordCard.voice: Three lines of teaching: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind, the Dhammapada's summary of the teaching of the Buddhas. Easy to know, hard to do.

orig.note: Pali, in roman letters with marks: not doing any evil, the first words of verse 183.

carryVoice: The line to keep: avoid, do, purify, in that order. Nine days with the verses, and the master's still in his tree.
